blocks.text: The next chapter will talk more about this: the difference between a limit in potential and a limit in actuality, which is the difference between the *kelim* and the *tikunim*. A limit in potential is a *kli*; a limit in actuality is a *tikun*. And later, in the chapters of the thirties, it will be discussed how *osios* (letters) are called both *kelim* and *levushim* (garments): the same idea he is explaining here, that the inner side of it is a *kli* and the outer side is a *levush*. Before you make an actual movement, the fact that it can transform your power into a particular movement is a *tikun*, whereas that your entire essential power can rest there is a *kli*. That is the difference between a *kli* and a *tikun* or a *levush*: a *kli* holds the whole thing, and a *levush* is only one expression of it.

blocks.title: The fireman's hat and the store uniform
blocks.text: If you put on your fireman hat and coat and everything, now we see you as a fireman. Or you can take that off and put on one of those white coats with a stethoscope. Different clothes are like putting on different roles, and we see you as that thing: "Oh, what is he? Oh, he's a doctor." That is not your *etzem*. Your clothes express only one thing that you do, *davka* how people should relate to you. That is the main idea of clothes, like a uniform: people should know how to relate to you. Doctors dress a certain way so that you know who the doctor is and who is not. In a store, how do you know whom to ask where to find something? They wear the store uniform. If they did not, you would ask some customer, and he would say, "Oh, I'm sorry sir, I don't work here." So there is an idea here, and now it kind of becomes a lost thing.

blocks.title: The nephew's wedding
blocks.text: He does not know; most people do not appreciate this and are not doing it on purpose. They are just trying to copy the Rebbe, like a little kid who wants to dress up and puts on his father's clothes. Like his nephew, who likes to dress up in different things. The other day Rabbi Walters came there, and he was all dressed up, with his father's hat on, wearing his Shabbos suit, vest or coat or something. He asked him what he was all dressed up for. He said he is doing a wedding, he is having a wedding: he likes to dress up, he is going to a wedding, or he is the groom, or he pretends to be doing a wedding. That is kind of what it is like for most people: they are just copying the Rebbe.

blocks.title: How the Rebbe dressed
blocks.text:
But the real idea of clothes is different. The Rebbe did not just copy the way the Previous Rebbe dressed; actually he did not dress like the Previous Rebbe. When he was a chassid and wanted people to leave him alone and not make a big deal out of him, he *davka* dressed like somebody modern, and people left him alone. When he wanted people *davka* to come to him and know that he is the Rebbe, he dressed like a Rebbe.

And it says that when *Moshiach* comes, the people who are prophets will wear long coats, a long thing like the High Priest would wear, so that people will know to go ask them questions. That is why the Rebbe said that people who are mentors and heads of yeshivas should wear long coats all day, every day.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 54, the chapter's last tape, reads no line: it goes on with the difference between a kli and a tikun (lines 33-41), and is placed under the chapter's last line.

blocks.text: Why? So people will know that they are somebody to ask questions about these kinds of things. People say, "Oh, they don't want to, they're humble, who am I?" "It's a kind of a stupid humility." That is your job. If you want to do your job well, wear the clothes, because it helps you do your job; and if you do not want to do that job, then *davka* do not. On the other hand, people who are not doing that job are afraid to take off their clothes: "Oh, if I take off the clothes I'm not..." But being a chassid is not wearing a long coat.

blocks.title: The farmer in Kfar Chabad
blocks.text: Let's say somebody is a farmer: you can be a chassid wearing jeans and a flannel shirt, and a straw hat for that matter. Like what's his name, Donin, Yehuda Donin, Yisroel? The guy who lived in Kfar Chabad, who was a farmer. The Rebbe called him a true Jew, or something like that. He was this rough guy, he would curse and things, and he would give a class in *Chassidus* every day. He wanted to go out on a mission, or to do something holy, and the Rebbe told him, Rabbi Walters thinks, *davka* to be a farmer. So he had a tractor in Kfar Chabad.

blocks.text: But nowadays people, he does not know. There is a certain thing of the chassidic dress, but people totally do not have any consciousness of what they are doing, and they are not doing it with any purpose, really. It just becomes, "Oh, it's an *inyan*." The outer thing becomes its own *inyan*, and it loses the inner side totally. Even when it would be appropriate to change the way a person dresses, they just follow; they feel it is an essential thing. So that is the idea of clothes.

blocks.title: So we won't get burned
blocks.text: So too, it says that at the splitting of the Sea they saw G-d as a young warrior, and at the giving of the Torah as an old sage: He put on different clothes. That is the idea of *tikunim*. But the difference is that in the *mashal* the clothes fix you, and in the *nimshal* they fix us, so that we can see Him. A fireman puts on heat-protecting things so that he will not get burned by the fire, "but G-d puts on the clothes so we won't get burned by Him." So in a way it is reversed.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 54, the chapter's last tape, reads no line: it goes on with the difference between a kli and a tikun (lines 33-41), and is placed under the chapter's last line.

blocks.text: In a way it is more like the eye, or the brain: you have the idea, but it is too big. If G-d were revealed the way He is essentially, we would not feel that we are separate from Him. So first the vessels just reveal G-d within them. That is why the vessels of *Atzilus* are still called *Elokus* (G-dliness): His whole *etzem* can be revealed there; they still have free choice, they can create *yesh me'ayin* (something from nothing), still G-dly, so to speak. That is why it is called the end and the *Ein Sof* (the Infinite), as will be explained later.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 54, the chapter's last tape, reads no line: it goes on with the difference between a kli and a tikun (lines 33-41), and is placed under the chapter's last line.

blocks.text:
On the other hand, they are also the source of the limit, the *memutza* (a middle) between *Atzilus* and *Beriya*, *Yetzira* and *Asiya*, because their outer side makes the actual limit within time and space, so that G-d reveals Himself in a certain way. The idea of Creator, the vessel of *chesed* of *Atzilus*, reveals G-d's essence: He is the Creator. But when He actually uses it to create something, G-d reveals Himself in a particular way. He creates something and that is a revelation of Him, but the creation is now something limited.

So the vessels bridge the gap. Their inner side reveals Him, His whole *etzem*, because only G-d could create; their outer side, the revelation of that vessel, is an actual limited thing that we could know. When G-d chose to reveal Himself as a Creator, that gave creation a meaning, a reason to exist: it can be a revelation of G-d, as an example of His ability to create, which is an example of Him.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 54, the chapter's last tape, reads no line: it goes on with the difference between a kli and a tikun (lines 33-41), and is placed under the chapter's last line.

blocks.text: That is the idea of the vessels: the inner side reveals the whole *etzem*, and the outer side gives a place for *Beriya*, *Yetzira* and *Asiya* to exist as something separate from G-d. But they are not really separate; they are seen as connected, even though they are limited.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 54, the chapter's last tape, reads no line: it goes on with the difference between a kli and a tikun (lines 33-41), and is placed under the chapter's last line.

blocks.text: The only thing is that *Adam Kadmon* does not yet relate to the particulars, like a tree. But in a way it does. With a tree, there is this great wisdom in every single detail; you see the infinite wisdom in the tree. And that it is an infinitely complex system, everything different and all the parts working together, no two parts the same, is more like *bina*; the wisdom is like the *chachma*.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 55, the first "More on Chapter 28" tape, reads no line: it explains the lights of Atzilus before they go into the vessels, the ten sefiros b'li ma of lines 6-9 and 41, and is placed under the chapter's last line.

blocks.text: Then there is the essential will: you see that the tree wants to grow and to be a tree in a certain form. Why? Where does it think it is growing? What does it want? It wants to get close to the sun. Why? "Such a waste. You know, you ever go look at trees and plants and think like they're idiots? Where do they think they're going?" They grow and grow and grow so they can get close to the sun and get more light, and there is no end; it is a totally meaningless, useless thing. The only one who benefits from it is us. So you obviously see that there is a will there, a big push making it want to do that, but it does not make sense that it is really the tree's will. You see G-d's will pushing the tree.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 55, the first "More on Chapter 28" tape, reads no line: it explains the lights of Atzilus before they go into the vessels, the ten sefiros b'li ma of lines 6-9 and 41, and is placed under the chapter's last line.

blocks.text:
And you see it being created anew every single second. If you really look into the tree, every single moment it is being created anew: all its molecules revert to nothing and come back into existence every moment; if you go down to the atomic level you see that. Or in a lesser way: every single day the plant has renewed energy, it is constantly being renewed, stopping and coming back, and every year it loses its leaves and kind of dies, and then comes back. But really it happens every single moment, the more you look into it on an essential, constant level.

He points that out because that is the main place where you see the level of light he is talking about now: the lights of *Atzilus* before they go into the *kelim*.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 55, the first "More on Chapter 28" tape, reads no line: it explains the lights of Atzilus before they go into the vessels, the ten sefiros b'li ma of lines 6-9 and 41, and is placed under the chapter's last line.

blocks.text: The way you see it every day or every year is the way it is already enclothed in *kelim*. But the essential light of it, before it comes into the *kelim*, is infinite. Even scientifically, if you really look into the tree at the molecular or subatomic level, they see how every single moment it is being recreated. But that is not revealed in a vessel, and that is why you do not see it so much; you have to look deeper. What is revealed in a vessel, a limited vessel, is that it is renewed every day and every year. Right now we are talking about the lights before they go into the vessel: that G-d gives it new life not just every day or every year, but every single moment, essentially, in an infinite way.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 55, the first "More on Chapter 28" tape, reads no line: it explains the lights of Atzilus before they go into the vessels, the ten sefiros b'li ma of lines 6-9 and 41, and is placed under the chapter's last line.

blocks.text: It is just as a person has an infinite ability for intellect, and when it goes into the brain it comes out in particular ideas. And even the whole desire to express intellect in everything he will come across, the infinite light that goes into the brain, comes out because of his *Adam Kadmon*: he decided he wants to be a smart person, and so he wants to express it. So too, because G-d decided to reveal Himself through wisdom, there is this inherent light that wants to reveal His wisdom infinitely in everything. That is not manifest to us. It is manifest through the vessels, in limited ways and in certain things, so that we see it more in certain areas than in others, even though, if we look into it and think about it, we will realize that G-d's wisdom is manifest infinitely in everything.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 55, the first "More on Chapter 28" tape, reads no line: it explains the lights of Atzilus before they go into the vessels, the ten sefiros b'li ma of lines 6-9 and 41, and is placed under the chapter's last line.

blocks.question: Rocks don't seem to have that renewal as much?
blocks.text: That is one of the things: there is less of a revelation of G-dliness. You see the renewal most in people, then in animals, then in plants, and least in inanimate objects, because in inanimate objects the vessel is the dominant thing, and you do not see the light as much; in a person you see the light most. Nevertheless, if you really look into the rock you will still see it, and you do not even have to go to the molecular level. Rocks are also kind of like fruits coming out of trees: diamonds are made by mountains and the earth, and the world is constantly renewing those elements as they get used up, washed away and corroded. Even the surface of the earth is constantly changing and renewing. Watch some nature show: rivers carve out huge valleys, the wind erodes, it changes constantly, even the hardest rock, all a cycle, "like the living planet." They show fast-forward videos taken over a month of the same place, and you see it dying and coming back: eaten away by the elements and broken down, and rebuilt into a new rock. It is just much slower.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 55, the first "More on Chapter 28" tape, reads no line: it explains the lights of Atzilus before they go into the vessels, the ten sefiros b'li ma of lines 6-9 and 41, and is placed under the chapter's last line.

blocks.text: In between there is the light of *Atzilus*, which comes out from *Adam Kadmon*. There is the way it is expressed through vessels, limited ways, which is the way we appreciate it most. There is the fact that G-d chose to reveal Himself through it. And in between there is this light: that the thing inherently exists in everything. Once G-d connected Himself to it, since He is infinite and essential, and not for any reason, once G-d connected Himself to the idea of *chesed*, of creating something, everything is inherently created by G-d in an infinite way. That is just the nature of things, not limited to a particular instance or to certain circumstances.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 55, the first "More on Chapter 28" tape, reads no line: it explains the lights of Atzilus before they go into the vessels, the ten sefiros b'li ma of lines 6-9 and 41, and is placed under the chapter's last line.

blocks.text: In the vessel of *chesed* it is. At certain times it is revealed and at certain times not; some things you see as creation and some things you do not. But in the light of *chesed* of *Atzilus* it is infinite: if you look into the world, you see it as a logical reality, axiomatic, that everything inherently must be recreated every single moment by G-d. That comes from the *chesed* of *Adam Kadmon*: G-d associated Himself with this *midda* (attribute), which gave it His properties. Then G-d chose the vessel of *chesed* of *Atzilus* to manifest it in certain ways, so that certain things manifest the idea of *chesed* more openly. That was so that it should not be the way of *Tohu* (the world of Chaos), or else each of the *middos* would be seen equally as infinite all the time, and you would not be able to appreciate one over the other.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 55, the first "More on Chapter 28" tape, reads no line: it explains the lights of Atzilus before they go into the vessels, the ten sefiros b'li ma of lines 6-9 and 41, and is placed under the chapter's last line.

blocks.text: So G-d put them in the vessels of *Atzilus*, which give each one its own place: certain aspects of reality reveal these different lights to us more strongly. When we look at certain aspects of the tree we see mainly the *chachma*; at other aspects, mainly the *chesed*. But really you could take any one of these, *chachma* or *chesed*, and use it to explain all the aspects of the tree, because it really extends to everything. You do not have to call the wisdom wisdom; you could call it *chesed*.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 55, the first "More on Chapter 28" tape, reads no line: it explains the lights of Atzilus before they go into the vessels, the ten sefiros b'li ma of lines 6-9 and 41, and is placed under the chapter's last line.

blocks.text: When you see all the amazing detail of the tree, you do not have to say that it is the expression of G-d's wisdom. You can say that it is an expression of G-d's creation, that He is creating in all these different ways: the system, the way the tree works, the whole idea of the wisdom, that it seems graceful and beautiful to you, all of it is being created. That is the thing of *Tohu*, where you see them all as infinite and equal. When they went into the vessels, we came to see certain aspects of G-dliness individually, in different things and in different ways, which lets us focus on certain things and appreciate them more and less.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 55, the first "More on Chapter 28" tape, reads no line: it explains the lights of Atzilus before they go into the vessels, the ten sefiros b'li ma of lines 6-9 and 41, and is placed under the chapter's last line.

blocks.title: A walk in the woods
blocks.text:
Now we see only one at a time, and in a limited way; sometimes we see G-dliness more and sometimes less. When Rabbi Walters walks through the woods here, he sees G-dliness more easily than when he is sitting in his house or in the synagogue. He sees the wisdom and beauty and all the amazing things in nature, more life, more vitality and more G-dliness, than when he is looking at plasterboard walls that are man-made. To him that covers up the G-dliness, because he does not see the direct involvement of G-d; it went through so many more intermediaries of man. Even though man is just manipulating the things G-d made, and people's intellect and abilities are totally given by G-d, so that He made the house too, not just the tree, he does not see it as much.

And in a way G-d's wisdom is even more expressed in his house, because He is able to use people and all these extra intermediaries to make the house come out. It is not direct, so G-d has to pull all these strings and arrange all these things to influence the architects so that it comes out this way.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 56, the second "More on Chapter 28" tape, reads no line: it goes on with the lights of Atzilus as the ten sefiros b'li ma (lines 6-9 and 41), and is placed under the chapter's last line.

blocks.text: He once heard that you are not supposed to contemplate man-made things for the greatness of the Creator. But he thinks that if you turn it into a G-d-made thing, it is different. He thinks the point is that you should not go look at a skyscraper, be impressed by how big it is and say, "Wow, G-d's even greater," because really you are being impressed by human achievement. That is what he heard; he never saw it, so he cannot really say, and sometimes people mess up the context, but he can see that there is probably something to it. You can make an *inyan* out of everything, for sure.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 56, the second "More on Chapter 28" tape, reads no line: it goes on with the lights of Atzilus as the ten sefiros b'li ma (lines 6-9 and 41), and is placed under the chapter's last line.

blocks.text: On the other hand, he really likes going out to nature. When you go to a city, man covered over G-dliness with cement and wood and whatever, and *mamash* makes a *kelipa* (lit. husk; what conceals G-dliness) that makes it harder to see, because they cover it up with all their stuff.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 56, the second "More on Chapter 28" tape, reads no line: it goes on with the lights of Atzilus as the ten sefiros b'li ma (lines 6-9 and 41), and is placed under the chapter's last line.

blocks.text: That is like *chachma* of *Adam Kadmon* and *chachma* of *Atzilus*: the way you see the wisdom in the tree, and that it comes in a specific form, what we know as wisdom and order. That certain things seem orderly and logical to us: really G-d created that, and people do not realize it. G-d created the whole idea of order, that certain things are graceful to us, and certain things strike us as logical, orderly and beautiful, as having a design. Nowadays people are starting to expand their view of that, to appreciate that chaos itself has an order, the whole chaos theory, that there is a beauty in it. They are starting to fudge the whole line between order and chaos, seeing how both of them have both in them, and that paradox is in a way the greatest beauty of it.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 56, the second "More on Chapter 28" tape, reads no line: it goes on with the lights of Atzilus as the ten sefiros b'li ma (lines 6-9 and 41), and is placed under the chapter's last line.

blocks.text: This whole deeper view of things all stems from the fact that really G-d creates the whole idea of what is logical and beautiful and graceful. So really it is not inherently an order; it is really a chaos, because G-d is just choosing to do whatever He wants, and He chose to make it logical. Why should a certain thing be logical? It is hard for people to realize that. "Like 1 1 is 2": that we see that as obviously so and very logical is just because G-d made us that way. Why should it be? "It'd be a whole different reality if G-d made different *kelim* in *Atzilus*."
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 56, the second "More on Chapter 28" tape, reads no line: it goes on with the lights of Atzilus as the ten sefiros b'li ma (lines 6-9 and 41), and is placed under the chapter's last line.

blocks.text: That is why the lights of *Atzilus* are still called the ten *sefiros b'li ma*. Compared to *Adam Kadmon* they are already very tangible: in the lights of *Atzilus*, before they come into the vessel, G-d is revealed as infinitely wise, as essentially a creator. The light of *chesed* of *Atzilus* is that G-d is inherently, essentially a creator, and so everything is essentially created by Him every single moment, every aspect of it. Seemingly that light is very limited compared to *Adam Kadmon*'s point of view, where G-d was higher than the whole thing of creation and chose to connect Himself to it. Now you are looking at G-d as inherently this creator; you are defining G-d by that quality.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 56, the second "More on Chapter 28" tape, reads no line: it goes on with the lights of Atzilus as the ten sefiros b'li ma (lines 6-9 and 41), and is placed under the chapter's last line.

blocks.text: Nevertheless, we say that it is *b'li ma* compared to the vessels of *Atzilus*. That G-d is inherently a creator is still infinite and undefined compared to the particular creations G-d is going to use to manifest that quality of Himself. The reason that light can be infinite like that is that G-d connected it to His essence. Just as He is infinite, not limited, with free choice, this quality now takes on all those characteristics: it is infinite, it is not bound to anything, and it can come out in any way He chooses. So within this quality it is *b'li ma* and infinite. Even though it is just like a color, something not essentially connected to G-d's essence, once He chose to connect Himself to it, it becomes an intrinsic thing and takes on the qualities of G-d's essence by way of association.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 56, the second "More on Chapter 28" tape, reads no line: it goes on with the lights of Atzilus as the ten sefiros b'li ma (lines 6-9 and 41), and is placed under the chapter's last line.

blocks.question: How do we see it in a tree?
blocks.text:
The tree is really just one example of the way a tree could be. G-d could use the same creative ability, the same wisdom, to make it in infinite ways. We see the inherent ability behind it, and that the tree is just one representation, one example of G-d's ability to make a tree, and we realize that really G-d could do it in infinite different ways. That is where we go from the fact that there are so many different trees, each one different, constantly growing new things: that diversity shows us more and more that it is really infinite. It is a creative ability, and G-d chooses how it is going to come out; it is not a system, like a machine that pumps these things out in a strict order. It really has a certain element of chaos and of free choice.

But when you ask him to give you an example within the tree, he is showing you how it is revealed within the vessels: within the vessel you see that behind it is the light, whereas the light itself is just the concept of it, which is what he told you first.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 56, the second "More on Chapter 28" tape, reads no line: it goes on with the lights of Atzilus as the ten sefiros b'li ma (lines 6-9 and 41), and is placed under the chapter's last line.

blocks.text: The fact that inherently everything must be recreated every single moment by G-d, that this is just the way reality is, is the real light of *chesed* of *Atzilus*. The way you see that in a tree is where that light is manifest through the vessel of *Atzilus* into *Beriya*, *Yetzira* and *Asiya*: a glimmer of a glimmer of a glimmer. Nevertheless, it is important to see it there, because there you see it in a *prat*, and when you see it in the *pratim*, it becomes close to you. But then you have to extrapolate the *klal* from the *pratim*: the real thing you are trying to recognize is the general truth, not just in a tree, but that the nature of reality is that it depends on G-d to be recreated every single moment. That is the *klal*.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 56, the second "More on Chapter 28" tape, reads no line: it goes on with the lights of Atzilus as the ten sefiros b'li ma (lines 6-9 and 41), and is placed under the chapter's last line.

blocks.text: The *hisbonenus* (contemplation) is that you want to try to see: how do I see that in a tree? How do I see that in a bug? How do I see that in the stock market? When you see how each of these things reflects that truth in a way you can actually point to, the truth becomes much more apparent and much more real to you, because you see it in the *pratim*. Nevertheless, the *pratim* are only a reflection of it, as it is enclothed in the *kelim* and goes into the *osios* of thought, speech and action, all the way down to *Asiya*: a glimmer of a glimmer of a glimmer. But when you find the way it is reflected in the *prat*, you really see the *klal* much more truly. So you need both. You need to recognize the *klal*, which is what we are doing now, and after you understand the *klal*, contemplate the *pratim* and see it in the tree.
